enum: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies
JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Can't tell / Not directly applicable: No refusals, non-response, or participant withdrawal during the primary fieldwork are reported. A July 2011 follow-up site visit (PDF p. 24, p. 402) describes settlement-level infrastructure updates rather than longitudinal tracking of the original 32 households.
cross_tool_domains.confounding: Not directly applicable (qualitative descriptive/interpretive study making no causal effect estimates): Contextually, differences between the two slums are situated alongside caste/tribal composition (80% Scheduled Tribe Lambada with formerly nomadic roots in Banjara Colony vs. mixed caste composition in Vajpayeenagar), municipal notification status, housing construction under VAMBAY, water supply mode, and black cotton soil conditions, though these structural factors co-vary across only two settlements.
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Moderate / Descriptive only: Legal-administrative distinctions central to urban slum governance—specifically 'Notified Slum' status (bringing Vajpayeenagar within government development schemes) versus 'Non-Notified Slum' status (Banjara Colony), alongside public programmes (Integrated Low-Cost Sanitation [ILCS], Valmiki Ambedkar Awas Yojana [VAMBAY], Total Sanitation Campaign [TSC], and rural ASHA sanitary-napkin subsidies)—are identified contextually (PDF pp. 5, 10–11, 24–25; pp. 383, 388–389, 402–403), but statutory provisions, municipal notification rules, tenure rights, and scheme eligibility criteria are not doctrinally cited or systematically operationalized.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Moderate concern / Can't tell: Multi-method qualitative collection (FGDs, guided-checklist interviews, participatory wealth ranking, and direct observation) allowed cross-checking of stated norms against observed practices (e.g., refuting men's claims that only literate residents bathe regularly, PDF p. 15, p. 393). However, absence of topic guides, audio-recording/transcription/translation protocols, FGD counts, fieldwork dates, and interviewer gender/positionality disclosures when probing sensitive topics (open defecation, bathing, sexual harassment, menstruation) creates substantial risk of social desirability and observer bias.
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Adequate for qualitative lived experience, weak for physical/health outcomes: Women's sanitation definitions, daily hygiene time burdens, gendered cleaning division of labour, privacy/safety stressors during open defecation and bathing, and menstrual hygiene constraints are richly documented through interviews, FGDs, and observation (PDF pp. 7–23, pp. 385–401). Conversely, water quality ('safe for drinking', 'salty'), septic seepage, and health consequences (diarrhoea, reproductive tract infections) rely on resident perceptions and informal observation rather than microbiological, clinical, or engineering measurements.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Moderate concern / Can't tell: No study protocol or systematic qualitative coding framework is reported. Although 'individual questionnaires' are mentioned in the Methodology section (PDF p. 7, p. 385), systematic questionnaire tabulations are omitted (apart from approximate task times for six named women in Table 2 and an isolated '25 per cent' figure in Box 3), creating risk of selective narrative illustration, partially mitigated by explicit reporting of divergent respondent perspectives (e.g., PDF p. 22, p. 400).
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: Can't tell / Moderate concern: Two Hyderabad slums were purposively contrasted (notified Vajpayeenagar in Qutbullapur municipality vs. non-notified Banjara Colony in LB Nagar municipality), and 32 households were stratified across four community-defined Asset and Vulnerability categories ('Eight households from each of the four economic categories were selected in both these localities, a total of 32 households'), supplemented by FGDs across gender and age groups (PDF pp. 5–7, pp. 383–385). However, within-stratum household selection mechanics, FGD recruitment procedures, gatekeeper roles, and refusal rates are unreported.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was there a clear statement of the aims of the research?
domain_ratings.justification: The Abstract (PDF p. 3, p. 381) and Introduction/Methodology (PDF pp. 4–5, 7; pp. 382–383, 385) clearly articulate the research goal: examining what appropriate sanitation and personal hygiene mean to poor and vulnerable women in two Hyderabad urban slums, documenting gendered sanitation labour, privacy/dignity and menstrual hygiene challenges, and informing women-centred sanitation programme design.
domain_ratings.where_found: [PDF Page 3 of 26] Abstract (p. 381); [PDF Pages 4–5 of 26] Introduction (pp. 382–383); [PDF Page 7 of 26] Methodology (p. 385)

domain_ratings.justification: A participatory qualitative methodology is appropriate for investigating locally perceived definitions of cleanliness (shubram, acchocha), lived experiences of shame, fear, and modesty during open defecation and bathing, intra-household gender norms, and cultural practices around childbirth, death pollution, and menstruation among marginalized urban slum residents.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the research design appropriate to address the aims of the research?
domain_ratings.justification: The comparative two-slum participatory field design—contrasting a notified slum (Vajpayeenagar) and a non-notified slum (Banjara Colony), stratifying households into four community-defined Asset and Vulnerability categories (Table 1), and combining FGDs, guided-checklist interviews across 32 households, and direct observation—is explicitly justified following Chambers (1983) to move away from 'survey slavery' and amplify heterogeneous urban poor voices.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the recruitment strategy appropriate to the aims of the research?
domain_ratings.justification: While the authors report selecting 32 households stratified across four community-defined economic categories in the two slums alongside FGDs with women, adolescent girls, school-going children, and men, they provide no explanation of how specific households within each stratum or FGD participants were identified and recruited (e.g., random vs. convenience vs. Resident Community Volunteer referral), why these two specific Hyderabad slums were selected, or whether any invited residents declined participation.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the data collected in a way that addressed the research issue?
domain_ratings.justification: Although multiple complementary field methods are named (participatory wealth categorisation, FGDs, guided-checklist household interviews, individual questionnaires, direct observation, and a July 2011 revisit), essential data-collection mechanics are omitted: the paper does not report when initial fieldwork took place, how many FGDs were held, the content of the guided checklist or questionnaire, how interviews/FGDs were recorded (audio recording vs. field notes) or translated from Telugu/Lambadi, who conducted interviews on sensitive topics, or whether thematic saturation was assessed.
domain_ratings.where_found: [PDF Page 7 of 26] Methodology (p. 385); [PDF Page 24 of 26] A Summing Up (p. 402); [PDF Page 25 of 26] Acknowledgements (p. 403)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Has the relationship between researcher and participants been adequately considered?
domain_ratings.justification: Beyond noting an intention to conduct fieldwork 'at the convenience of the respondents' (PDF p. 7, p. 385), the authors include no reflexivity or positionality discussion examining how the researchers' gender (including a male lead author), class/caste background, or institutional affiliation influenced rapport, disclosure, or observation regarding intimate topics such as open defecation, bathing in public, marital labour disputes, and menstrual hygiene.
domain_ratings.where_found: [PDF Page 7 of 26] Methodology (p. 385); absent throughout full text

domain_ratings.domain_name: Have ethical issues been taken into consideration?
domain_ratings.justification: There is no mention of institutional ethics review, informed consent procedures, or confidentiality protections anywhere in the article. Moreover, the text and Table 2 repeatedly publish full personal and family/caste names alongside specific slum locations for vulnerable women recounting stigmatized and intimate experiences (open defecation, fear of sexual assault, marital conflict, and menstrual cloth disposal) without indicating that pseudonyms were used or that explicit consent to be named was obtained.
domain_ratings.where_found: [PDF Page 7 of 26] Methodology (p. 385); named respondents on [PDF Pages 10–11, 13–22 of 26] including Table 2 (pp. 388–389, 391–400)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the data analysis sufficiently rigorous?
domain_ratings.justification: The article provides no description of how qualitative interview, FGD, questionnaire, or observational data were organised, coded, or synthesised into themes, nor who performed the analysis. Although findings are richly illustrated with verbatim participant quotes and occasionally note divergent cases (e.g., minority views on changing menstrual cloths outdoors, PDF p. 22, p. 400), analytic rigor cannot be verified from the text.
domain_ratings.where_found: [PDF Page 7 of 26] Methodology (p. 385); Results sections [PDF Pages 7–23 of 26] (pp. 385–401)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Is there a clear statement of findings?
domain_ratings.justification: Findings are clearly and coherently presented across thematic sections covering local definitions of sanitation across economic strata (Box 1), structural/soil defects of ILCS latrines (Box 2), demand for private toilets, bathing and handwashing habits, gendered domestic cleaning burdens (Table 2, Box 3), and childbirth, bereavement, and menstrual hygiene needs, with clear synthesis linked back to policy aims in 'A Summing Up' (PDF pp. 23–25, pp. 401–403), including discrepant observations and minority viewpoints.
domain_ratings.where_found: [PDF Pages 7–25 of 26] What is Appropriate Sanitation? through A Summing Up (pp. 385–403)

domain_ratings.domain_name: How valuable is the research? (Narrative assessment)
domain_ratings.justification: Narrative assessment: The study offers valuable empirical insight into the gendered 'last mile' of urban slum sanitation in India, demonstrating how housing-scheme demolitions (VAMBAY) of existing ILCS latrines, technical design failures (unlined/seeping pits in black cotton soil without municipal underground sewerage), non-notified slum exclusion, and neglect of bathing privacy and menstrual water/disposal needs undermine nominal sanitation coverage. Transferability and evidentiary weight are nonetheless tempered by its restriction to two Hyderabad slums and substantial omissions in sampling, data-recording, analytic, reflexive, and ethical reporting.
domain_ratings.rating: Valuable contextual and policy contribution, tempered by reporting and ethical limitations (narrative)
domain_ratings.where_found: [PDF Pages 3, 10–12, 21–25 of 26] Abstract, ILCS/open defecation analysis, Menstruation, and A Summing Up (pp. 381, 388–390, 399–403)

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: This participatory qualitative field study investigates perceptions, practices, and gendered burdens of sanitation and personal hygiene among poor and vulnerable residents in two urban slums of Hyderabad, India—Vajpayeenagar (a notified slum) and Banjara Colony (a non-notified slum)—as part of a DFID-supported University of Southampton multi-country project. Evaluated with the CASP Qualitative Checklist, the study exhibits clear research aims (Q1: Yes), an appropriate qualitative participatory methodology (Q2: Yes), a well-matched comparative and economically stratified design across four community-defined Asset and Vulnerability categories (Q3: Yes), and a coherent, richly illustrated presentation of thematic findings including divergent perspectives (Q9: Yes) with clear relevance to urban WASH governance (Q10). However, it warrants an overall judgment of moderate-to-high methodological concern (3 'Can't tell' and 2 'No' items across Q1–Q9) due to major reporting and ethical deficiencies: the text does not explain how the 32 interviewed households or FGD participants were recruited within strata (Q4: Can't tell), omits fieldwork dates, FGD counts, interview guides, recording/translation procedures, and saturation checks (Q5: Can't tell), provides zero description of qualitative coding or data analysis (Q8: Can't tell), lacks any researcher reflexivity on gender/caste/class positionality despite intimate subject matter (Q6: No), and reports no ethical approval, informed consent, or anonymization while naming vulnerable women alongside their residential slums (Q7: No).
raw_response.overall_rating: Moderate-to-high methodological concern (3 Can't tell and 2 No items)
raw_response.study_design_identified: Participatory qualitative field study (comparative two-slum qualitative case study using focus group discussions, community Asset and Vulnerability categorisation, guided-checklist interviews with 32 stratified households, and direct observation)
raw_response.where_found_summary: Full text (26 PDF pages; journal pp. 381–404): Abstract on PDF p. 3 (p. 381); Introduction on PDF pp. 4–5 (pp. 382–383); Methodology and Table 1 on PDF pp. 5–7 (pp. 383–385); thematic qualitative findings, Boxes 1–3, and Table 2 on PDF pp. 7–23 (pp. 385–401); synthesis and July 2011 revisit in 'A Summing Up' on PDF pp. 23–25 (pp. 401–403); project provenance in Acknowledgements on PDF p. 25 (p. 403).
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: The study's primary empirical design is a participatory qualitative field investigation in two Hyderabad slums relying on focus group discussions (FGDs), community-developed wealth/vulnerability ranking (Table 1), in-depth household interviews using a guided checklist (n = 32 households), and behavioural observation, explicitly aiming 'to move away from "survey slavery" towards less rigid and less formal styles of information collection and collation' (PDF p. 7, p. 385). Although 'individual questionnaires' are mentioned in passing and approximate daily task durations are listed for six named women in Table 2, there is no quantitative survey sampling design, structured quantitative variable measurement, or statistical analysis constituting a quantitative empirical strand for MMAT. Accordingly, the CASP Qualitative Checklist is the single matching appraisal instrument under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1.
